summary: A paper submitted to the IPng effort arguing that the real need is a new version of TCP and UDP, not just a new IP. It was a contribution to the discussion and is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Someone says that to fix the internet we should also change the delivery rules on top, not just the addresses underneath.

questions: why change tcp and udp for ipng
why tcp udp depends on ip
subtitle: A proposal to make TCP and UDP protocol-independent by adding a transport layer address.

tldr.problem: IPv4 addresses are running out and IPng proposals focus only on changing IP layer, but TCP and UDP are tightly coupled to IP addresses in their checksums and socket structures. Each new IP version will require changes to TCP/UDP, complicating migration.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC proposes a new TCP and UDP that use a separate Transport Address (TA) instead of IP addresses. A TA would be a globally unique 64-bit identifier assigned to each TCP/UDP instance, making the transport layer protocol-independent. Multiple network layer protocols could run under the same TCP/UDP.
tldr.outcome: The proposal offers backward compatibility, incremental deployment, and decoupling of transport from network layers, but adds header overhead and the complexity of managing another global address space.

today: RFC 1705 remains an informational proposal and was never adopted as a standard. The actual IPng effort resulted in IPv6, and TCP/UDP were updated to support IPv6 without fundamental redesign (primarily changes to address handling and pseudo-header computation). The RFC's argument about layer independence and protocol decoupling remains academically valid, but the Internet community chose a more conservative evolution, updating TCP and UDP minimally rather than redesigning them. The proposal serves as a historical example of alternative architectural approaches considered during the IPng selection process.

sections.title: The Core Problem: Transport and Network Coupling
sections.content:
TCP and UDP were designed when IP was the only network layer in use. They are deeply coupled to IPv4:

  • A socket (the end of a connection) is formed by concatenating an IP address and a port number.
  • TCP and UDP checksums include the source and destination IP addresses in a pseudo-header, making them dependent on the network layer.

This tight coupling means that to deploy a new IP version (IPng), TCP and UDP must be respecified and re-implemented. The RFC argues this violates the OSI model's principle that layers should be independent of their neighbors. The authors propose instead to give TCP/UDP their own addressing: a Transport Address that identifies a TCP/UDP instance globally, independent of which IP version it uses.
sections.plainLanguage: Today's system is like saying 'call me at ZIP code 12345 plus room number 22'. If you move to a new ZIP code, both numbers change. The proposal is to say 'call me at number 99999, no matter what zip code I am in'.

sections.title: The IPng Problem and Historical Context
sections.content:
In the early 1990s, IPv4 address space was predicted to exhaust within 2–4 years. Class-B addresses (which organizations overallocate to avoid the constraint of Class-C) were being consumed rapidly. Routing table growth was also unsustainable. These pressures led the IETF to solicit IPng proposals.

However, every IPng proposal implicitly required changes to TCP and UDP. The RFC observes that this points to a design flaw: the transport layer should not depend on a specific network layer protocol. OSI and standard network architecture practice demand independence between layers. The authors note that the datalink layer (Ethernet, T1, etc.) is already protocol-independent from IP, so why should transport not be independent as well?
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet grew so fast that address numbers were running out. Everyone talked about changing the address system, but nobody realized they would also have to change how TCP works at the same time.

sections.title: Transport Addresses and Protocol Independence
sections.content:
A Transport Address (TA) is a globally unique 64-bit identifier composed of:

  • A 24-bit manufacturer code (potentially reusing IEEE 802.3 MAC address manufacturer IDs).
  • A 40-bit manufacturer-defined identifier, typically derived from the device's serial number.

This TA is assigned to each TCP/UDP instance and is fixed, independent of which IP address(es) or network layer the host uses. A host can have IPv4, IPng, or multiple network layer interfaces simultaneously, and the TA remains constant. DNS would be extended to support TA records (TA and reverse in-addr.tcp records), allowing applications to look up a host by domain name and get its TA, while the network layer separately looks up the IP address.
sections.plainLanguage: Like a person's national ID number: it does not change if you move to a different house or country. The post office (network layer) figures out the house address (IP), but your ID (TA) stays the same.

sections.title: The New TCP Header (TCPng)
sections.content:
The proposed TCPng header is larger than today's TCP header (48 bytes instead of 20) and includes:

  • Destination TA and Source TA (64 bits each): The globally unique transport addresses.
  • Destination Port and Source Port (28 bits each, with 4 bits for version): Port numbers, now larger than IPv4's 16 bits.
  • Window, Sequence, and Acknowledgment numbers (64 bits each): Larger than IPv4's 32 bits, to support high-bandwidth-delay networks.
  • Quality of Service (QoS) field (4 bits): Allows TCP to request service levels from the network layer.
  • Compatibility bit (C): When set, indicates the other end is unmodified TCPv4. The TCPng host sends a TCPv4-compatible header (20 bytes) with the compatibility bit, allowing gradual deployment.
  • Checksum: Computed over the TCPng header only, not a pseudo-header, removing dependence on IP addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Like a shipping label that says 'from person-ID 123 to person-ID 456, via whatever shipping company is available, not just FedEx'.

sections.title: Connection Setup and Multi-Protocol Support
sections.content:
When an application requests a connection, it passes a domain name to TCP (not an IP address). TCPng:

  1. Looks up the destination's TA via DNS.
  2. Builds a Transmission Control Block with the TAs instead of IP addresses.
  3. Passes the TA to the network layer, which looks up the IP address (or IPng address).
  4. Sends the packet via the appropriate network layer.

Multiple network layer instances can be configured, and TCP probes them in priority order until one responds 'yes, I can deliver to this TA'. A TCP capable of this becomes a transporter (similar to a router), forwarding TCP packets between different network layer protocols. This allows IPv4 and IPng to coexist and interwork transparently at the transport layer, without application-level gateways or tunneling.
sections.plainLanguage: A person at address 'New York' wants to contact a friend at address 'London'. The message is labeled 'from person 123 to person 456'. Any postal system that knows how to reach person 456 (whether by plane, ship, or truck) can deliver it.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Deployment
sections.content:
TCPng is designed for incremental deployment. An unmodified IPv4 TCP/IP host cannot initiate to a TCPng-only host, but a TCPng host can communicate with both TCPv4 and other TCPng hosts:

  • When talking to a TCPv4 host, TCPng sends a TCPv4-compatible header (20 bytes) with the compatibility bit set. The TA is placed in the IP address fields (zero-padded for the lower 32 bits of each TA).
  • When talking to another TCPng host, TCPng sends the full 48-byte header.
  • A TCPng host can use a transporter function to relay packets between a TCPv4-only peer and the rest of the network using IPng, maintaining connectivity without dual-stack requirements.

This avoids the 'dual-stack burden': hosts do not need to run both IPv4 and IPng simultaneously indefinitely. They can migrate to IPng and use TCP transporters to reach remaining IPv4-only hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: Old post offices still understand the old format, so you can send them old-style labels. New offices understand both old and new. Gradually, everyone migrates to the new system without anyone losing contact.
